# The Split Set Decides: Why Shrinking the Quadratic Sieve Makes It Slower

*How a tempting shortcut for factoring large numbers turned out to point exactly the wrong way — and what really controls the hunt for smooth numbers.*

---

## A machine for manufacturing squares

Suppose someone hands you a large odd number $N$ — say $N = 103{,}764{,}863$ — and asks for its factors. Trial division is hopeless at cryptographic sizes, so modern methods use a cleverer idea that goes back to Fermat and was turned into a practical algorithm by Carl Pomerance in the early 1980s: the **quadratic sieve**.

The idea runs as follows. If you can find two numbers $x$ and $y$ with

$$x^2 \equiv y^2 \pmod N, \qquad x \not\equiv \pm y \pmod N,$$

then $N$ divides $(x-y)(x+y)$ without dividing either factor, so $\gcd(x-y, N)$ is a proper factor of $N$. The whole game is to *manufacture* such a congruence of squares.

The sieve does it in two stages.

**Stage one: collect relations.** Look at the values of the polynomial

$$f(x) = x^2 - N$$

for $x$ just above $\sqrt N$. These values are fairly small, and now and then one of them factors completely into small primes — primes up to some bound $B$. Such a value is called **$B$-smooth**, and each one is a *relation*. Our example has $x = 10188$:

$$10188^2 - 103{,}764{,}863 = 30{,}481 = 11 \cdot 17 \cdot 163.$$

**Stage two: linear algebra.** Write each relation as a vector of exponents mod 2, one coordinate per prime in the "factor base". A product of relations is a perfect square exactly when its exponent vectors add up to zero mod 2. So we need a linear dependency over the two-element field $\mathbb{F}_2$, and linear algebra promises one as soon as the number of relations is larger than the number of coordinates.

Here is the trade-off every designer of the sieve has to face. Call the number of columns $Q$. More columns mean more relations to collect before the linear algebra is sure to succeed, and a bigger matrix to reduce. So a natural thought follows: **make $Q$ smaller.** Fewer columns, fewer relations needed, less work.

This article is about why that thought is backwards, and about the number-theoretic fact that settles it.

---

## The surprise: paying more for less

A campaign of experiments tested this "shrink $Q$" proposal head-on. The experimenters ran three independent sets of runs: a synthetic model, a model built around the Chinese Remainder Theorem, and a real single-polynomial quadratic sieve. All three used measuring tools that had been independently cross-checked.

One earlier observation held up: the ratio $Q/\pi(B)$, where $\pi(B)$ counts the primes up to $B$, really does correlate with the number of relations needed. The measured correlation was $+0.77$, and it was not an artefact. But it attaches to the wrong cost. What a factoring run actually *pays for* is the number of sieve positions examined, because that is where the computer time goes. Measured in positions, the cost turned out to **fall** as $Q$ grows. It fell monotonically, by factors from $2.4\times$ to $13.1\times$ depending on the design.

> **The design rule.** At a fixed smoothness bound $B$, the paid sieve length *decreases* as the factor base grows. Any proposal that shrinks the factor base in order to shrink the linear algebra is moving the wrong term.

You can watch this happen on a laptop. Take $N = 103{,}764{,}863$ and $B = 400$. The full factor base has $Q = 41$ usable primes. Now pretend you may only use the smallest $q$ of them, and count how many sieve positions you have to scan to collect $q+1$ relations:

| columns $q$ | positions scanned |
|---:|---:|
| 16 | 1,651 |
| 22 | 784 |
| 28 | 747 |
| 34 | 638 |
| 41 | 599 |

The smallest factor base needs fewer relations, yet it costs almost three times as much sieving.

### Why the sign flips

The reason is a mismatch between how the two sides grow. Adding one prime $p$ to a set of primes $S$ raises the number of relations you need by exactly **one**: the target is $|S|+1$. The number of smooth numbers, though, grows **multiplicatively**. Every $S$-smooth number $m \le X/p$ gives a new smooth number $p \cdot m \le X$. Writing $\Psi_S(X)$ for the count of integers in $[1,X]$ whose prime factors all lie in $S$, this gives

$$\Psi_{S\cup\{p\}}(X) \;\ge\; \Psi_S(X) + \Psi_S(X/p).$$

Measure the cost by the work model "positions per guaranteed dependency",

$$\mathrm{work}(S) = \frac{|S| + 1}{\Psi_S(X)}.$$

A short calculation shows that adding $p$ **does not increase the work** as soon as

$$(|S|+1)\cdot \Psi_S(X/p) \;\ge\; \Psi_S(X).$$

This is a very weak condition. Take $S=\{2,3\}$, $X = 100$, $p=5$. There are $\Psi_{\{2,3\}}(100) = 20$ numbers up to 100 built only from 2s and 3s, and $\Psi_{\{2,3\}}(20) = 10$ of them are at most 20. Since $3 \times 10 = 30 \ge 20$, the criterion holds. Indeed $\Psi_{\{2,3,5\}}(100) = 34$, and

$$\mathrm{work}(\{2,3,5\}) = \tfrac{4}{34} \approx 0.118 \;<\; \tfrac{3}{20} = 0.15 = \mathrm{work}(\{2,3\}).$$

One extra column costs $+1$ and buys a multiplicative gain. That is the sign flip in one line.

---

## The density that ignores Dickman

There is a classical way to predict how many smooth numbers to expect. Put $u = \log X / \log B$. The chance that a random integer near $X$ is $B$-smooth is roughly $\rho(u)$, where $\rho$ is the **Dickman function**. It equals 1 on $[0,1]$ and then falls off faster than exponentially: $\rho(2) \approx 0.31$, $\rho(3) \approx 0.049$, $\rho(4)\approx 0.0049$. Run-time analyses of factoring algorithms are built on it.

An earlier round of the same campaign had claimed that "the Dickman density survives measurement". The new experiments refine that claim sharply. When instances are compared at **matched** $u$, the correlation between $\log \rho(u)$ and the measured smooth density is

$$\operatorname{corr}(\log\rho,\ \text{density}) = +0.029,$$

which is essentially zero. The correlation with the split-prime ratio, by contrast, is

$$\operatorname{corr}(Q/\pi(B),\ \text{density}) = +0.882.$$

So Dickman's function correctly describes how the yield depends on $u$, but it is *blind* to the quantity that separates one modulus from another at the same $u$. Two numbers $N_1, N_2$ of the same size, sieved with the same bound $B$, can have very different yields. The deciding factor is how many primes up to $B$ are "friendly" to each $N$.

That claim can be made exact. The number of smooth sieve values in a window $[a,b]$ with $a^2 > N$ satisfies

$$\#\{x\in[a,b] : x^2-N \text{ is } B\text{-smooth}\} \;\le\; \bigl(\lfloor\log_2(b^2-N)\rfloor + 1\bigr)^{Q(N,B)}.$$

The exponent is $Q(N,B)$, **not** $\pi(B)$. A matching lower bound of the same exponential shape also holds: if the product of the primes in $S$ is at most $X$, then $\Psi_S(X) \ge 2^{|S|}$, because every product of distinct primes from $S$ counts. At a fixed size $X$, and hence a fixed $u$, the smooth count is squeezed between two functions that are exponential in the number of usable primes. Nothing else about $B$ enters.

---

## Which primes are "friendly"? Quadratic reciprocity enters

Why do only some primes count? Suppose a prime $r$ divides a sieve value $x^2 - N$. Then

$$x^2 \equiv N \pmod r,$$

so $N$ is a perfect square modulo $r$. If $r$ does not divide $N$, this says exactly that the **Legendre symbol** $(N/r)$ equals $+1$. (The Legendre symbol is $+1$ when $N$ is a nonzero square mod $r$, $-1$ when it is a non-square, and $0$ when $r \mid N$.)

> **Theorem (split-set forcing).** If a prime $r$ with $r \nmid N$ divides some value $x^2 - N$, then $(N/r) = +1$. Conversely, every prime $r$ for which $N$ is a square mod $r$ divides some $x^2 - N$. So the primes up to $B$ that the sieve can ever touch are *exactly* the **admissible** primes: those that divide $N$ (the "ramified" ones) together with those having $(N/r) = +1$ (the "split" ones).

The names come from algebraic number theory. The primes with $(N/r)=+1$ are the ones that split in the quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt N)$. The ones with $(N/r) = -1$, the **inert** primes, never divide any sieve value at all. Roughly half of all primes are inert for a given $N$. For our example $N$:

| $B$ | $\pi(B)$ | $Q(N,B)$ | inert |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 100 | 25 | 13 | 12 |
| 500 | 95 | 49 | 46 |
| 2000 | 303 | 133 | 170 |

The three prime factors of our example relation behave just as the theorem says: $(N/11) = (N/17) = (N/163) = +1$. In the real-sieve experiments, all **2,215 of 2,215** smooth values had prime support inside the split set.

This changes how the "shrink $Q$" proposal should be read. **$Q$ is not a free parameter.** Once you fix the polynomial $x^2 - N$ and the bound $B$, the sieve has already decided which columns exist: precisely the admissible primes, with $Q(N,B) + \#\{\text{inert primes} \le B\} = \pi(B)$. Leaving out admissible primes on purpose does shrink the matrix, but as we saw, it makes the sieve slower.

A second suggestion, which tried to use the Chinese Remainder Theorem to concentrate on a small set of residues, was ruled out twice over: once by enumerating every case, and once by an inequality on the prime-sum function. Since $\theta(R) = \sum_{p\le R}\log p$ must stay below $\ln N$ for the construction to make sense, the fraction $\pi(R)/\pi(B)$ of the factor base it could control tends to zero.

---

## Which way does the inequality point?

The linear-algebra stage hid a quieter confusion. Let $k_{\text{success}}$ be the number of relations you need before some subset of them first multiplies to a square, that is, the length of the shortest linearly dependent run of exponent vectors. A tempting chain of inequalities reads

$$k_{\text{success}} \;\le\; \operatorname{rank} + 1 \;\le\; Q + 1.$$

Is the first step backwards? The answer depends on *which* rank you mean, and both readings are true:

- If "rank" means the rank of the **prefix** of $k$ vectors at the moment it first becomes dependent, then dependence forces $\operatorname{rank} + 1 \le k$. At the first dependence the two sides meet exactly:

$$k_{\text{success}} \;=\; \operatorname{rank}(\text{first } k_{\text{success}} \text{ vectors}) + 1.$$

- If "rank" means the rank of **all** the relations collected, including any past $k_{\text{success}}$, then $k_{\text{success}} \le \operatorname{rank}(M)+1$ holds, because rank can only grow as rows are added.

Either way $k_{\text{success}} \le Q + 1$, and this is sharp: if the first $Q$ relations happen to be the standard basis vectors, the first dependency arrives at exactly $Q + 1$. The bound counts **relations**, though, not **positions**. It says nothing about how long you sieve to *find* those relations. That is why the linear-algebra bound gives no upper bound on the actual work. In experiments the ratio $k_{\text{success}}/Q$ came out near $0.78$, $0.71$ and $0.60$ at $B = 1024$, $2048$ and $4096$. Those values are properties of the instances; the algebra does not fix them.

---

## A bug that hides from honest tests

The campaign also turned up a cautionary tale for anyone who computes. Two rank routines in a widely used computer-algebra library — one general, one that claims to work over $\mathrm{GF}(2)$ — were found to return the rank over the **rationals** when asked for the rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Take the incidence matrix of a triangle:

$$T = \begin{pmatrix} 1&1&0\\ 0&1&1\\ 1&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Over $\mathbb{Q}$ it has rank 3. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ the three rows add up to zero, so the rank is 2. A sieve that trusted the wrong routine would report "no dependency yet" while a perfectly good square sat in its data.

Why did ordinary testing miss this? A clean answer comes from determinants. For a square integer matrix $A$:

- $A$ has full rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$ exactly when $\det A$ is **odd**;
- $A$ has full rank over $\mathbb{Q}$ exactly when $\det A \neq 0$.

> **Theorem (discriminating tests).** A square integer test matrix can tell a "rank over $\mathbb{Q}$" routine apart from a correct "rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$" routine on the full-rank question **if and only if its determinant is a nonzero even integer.**

The triangle has $\det T = 2$, which is why it catches the bug. A test suite made of identity matrices, triangular matrices and singular matrices has only odd or zero determinants, so it would pass the broken routine every time.

The error also runs in one direction only:

$$\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_2}(A) \;\le\; \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A) \quad\text{for every integer matrix } A.$$

The proof is a small piece of 2-adic reasoning. Suppose some vectors are independent mod 2 but satisfy an integer relation. If every coefficient of that relation is even, divide it by 2; this can be repeated only finitely often. Eventually some coefficient is odd, and the relation reduced mod 2 is a nontrivial mod-2 relation, which contradicts independence. So a rational-rank routine can only *over*-report the $\mathbb{F}_2$-rank, which means it can only *miss* dependencies, never invent them.

The lesson was put into practice: the team deliberately broke routines and checked that their tests caught them (a **mutation test**). In the team's words, without this, "validation passed" is unfalsifiable. The same discipline caught three more silent defects: a modular square-root routine with two bugs, a gcd step that mishandled exponents, and a log-sieve that ignored prime powers. It also caught a problem in the team's own reports. Two sample tables had been re-typed rather than regenerated from the stored records, and 10 of 16 rows matched no stored instance. The aggregate numbers were all exact. The rule that follows is to regenerate tables from primary data, never transcribe them.

---

## The road ahead: large primes

If $Q$ is fixed by the split set and shrinking it only hurts, how can one get past the collapse in yield? The open question now reads: *at a fixed $B$, can one avoid the yield collapse without shrinking the column space?*

One classical channel looks promising, and its algebra is now settled. Keep **partial relations**: sieve values that are smooth apart from a single "large prime" $\ell > B$. One partial on its own is useless, since $\ell$ would need a column of its own. But two partials with the **same** large prime multiply to

$$(s_1\ell)(s_2\ell) = s_1 s_2\,\ell^2,$$

and $\ell^2$ is already a square. So the pair behaves like an ordinary full relation in the **same** $\mathbb{F}_2^Q$ column space.

> **Theorem (large-prime congruence).** Suppose you hold $a$ full relations and $b$ partial relations, and among the partials there are $D$ distinct large primes. If
> $$Q < a + (b - D),$$
> then some nonempty collection of full relations and paired partials multiplies to a perfect square.

A toy example: columns $\{2,3\}$ (so $Q=2$), one full relation $6$, and partials $2\cdot101$, $3\cdot101$, $6\cdot101$. Here $a + (b-D) = 1 + (3-1) = 3 > 2$, and indeed

$$6 \cdot (3\cdot 101)(2\cdot 101) = (6\cdot 101)^2.$$

The question of *cost* thus becomes a **birthday problem**: how fast does the number of collisions $b - D$ grow? Simulations with large primes weighted like $1/\ell$ show the collision count growing roughly quadratically at first (about 1.2 collisions among 50 partials, 19 among 200, nearly 200 among 800). The conjecture for the next step is that the moment $a + (b-D)$ first exceeds $Q$ comes strictly earlier, in sieve positions, than the moment $a$ alone does.

---

## What it all means

The quadratic sieve has been studied for forty years, and at small scale it still holds surprises. Three lessons stand out.

1. **Count the right cost.** Fewer relations are not the same as less work. Positions scanned are what you pay for, and they fall as the factor base grows.
2. **Number theory sets the columns.** Quadratic residues, through the Legendre symbol, fix the factor base before any design choice is made. Smooth yield is governed by how many primes split, a quantity Dickman's $\rho(u)$ cannot see.
3. **Tests must be able to fail.** A test matrix with odd determinant cannot tell a field-of-two rank from a rational rank. Only mutation testing turns "validation passed" into evidence.

None of this produces a faster factoring method, and the authors say so plainly: no new algorithm came out of this, consistent with every earlier round. What it does produce is a clearer map. It shows which levers are real, which point the wrong way, and where the next idea, perhaps a collision of large primes, has room to work.

# The Split Set Decides: Factor-Base Size, Smooth Yield, and the Direction of the Linear-Algebra Bound in the Single-Polynomial Quadratic Sieve

**Aristotle**

*October 2026*

---

## Abstract

We study a design proposal for the single-polynomial quadratic sieve (QS): shrink the effective factor base, of size $Q$, so that fewer relations are needed for the linear-algebra step. We show that the proposal is misdirected on three independent grounds.

**(i) $Q$ is not a free parameter.** A prime $r \nmid N$ divides some sieve value $x^2-N$ if and only if the Legendre symbol $(N/r)$ equals $+1$. So the set of primes $\le B$ the sieve can ever reach is exactly the admissible set (ramified $\cup$ split), and $Q(N,B)=\pi(B)-\#\{\text{inert } r\le B\}$ is determined by $N$ and $B$.

**(ii) Smooth yield is governed by $Q$, not by $\pi(B)$.** For an arbitrary prime set $S$ we prove the exponential sandwich $2^{|S|}\le\Psi_S(X)\le(\lfloor\log_2X\rfloor+1)^{|S|}$ (the lower bound holds when $\prod S\le X$). We prove the multiplicative step $\Psi_{S\cup\{p\}}(X)\ge\Psi_S(X)+\Psi_S(\lfloor X/p\rfloor)$. We also prove the sieve-yield ceiling $\#\{x\in[a,b]: x^2-N\ \text{is } B\text{-smooth}\}\le(\lfloor\log_2(b^2-N)\rfloor+1)^{Q(N,B)}$.

**(iii) Paid work falls as $Q$ grows.** In the cost model $\mathrm{work}(S)=(|S|+1)/\Psi_S(X)$, adding a prime $p$ to $S$ does not raise the cost as soon as $(|S|+1)\,\Psi_S(\lfloor X/p\rfloor)\ge\Psi_S(X)$.

Empirically, the sieve positions actually examined fall monotonically in $Q$, by factors of $2.4\times$ to $13.1\times$. At matched $u=\log X/\log B$, the measured smooth density correlates with $Q/\pi(B)$ at $+0.882$ and with $\log\rho(u)$ at only $+0.029$.

We also settle a disputed direction in the linear-algebra bound. We prove the exact identity $k_{\rm success}=\operatorname{rank}(\text{prefix}_{k_{\rm success}})+1$, which shows $k_{\rm success}\le\operatorname{rank}(M)+1\le Q+1$ for the full collected matrix $M$, and that both bounds are sharp.

We characterize which integer test matrices can detect a rank routine that silently computes over $\mathbb{Q}$ instead of $\mathbb{F}_2$: exactly those with nonzero even determinant. We prove the error is one-sided, $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_2}\le\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Q}}$.

Finally, we prove the algebraic core of the large-prime variant. With $a$ full relations, $b$ partial relations and $D$ distinct large primes, $Q<a+(b-D)$ already forces a congruence of squares in the same $\mathbb{F}_2^Q$ column space. This reduces the cost question to a birthday-type collision count.

---

## 1. Introduction

The quadratic sieve factors an odd composite $N$ by producing a congruence $X^2\equiv Y^2\pmod N$ with $X\not\equiv\pm Y$. Its single-polynomial form has two phases:

1. **Relation collection.** Scan positions $x\ge\lceil\sqrt N\rceil$ and keep those for which $f(x)=x^2-N$ is $B$-smooth, meaning all its prime factors are $\le B$.
2. **Linear algebra.** Reduce the exponent vectors of the relations modulo 2 and find a nonempty subset summing to $0$ in $\mathbb{F}_2^{Q}$. Here $Q$ is the number of primes that can occur.

A dependency is guaranteed once more than $Q$ relations are held. A tempting optimization follows. If $Q$ could be lowered, fewer relations would be needed and the matrix would be smaller. We call this proposal **P4**. In a preceding round of experiments, the ratio $Q/\pi(B)$ correlated with the number of relations needed at $+0.77$, which seemed to support it.

This paper shows that P4 moves the wrong term. Our contributions are:

* **Split-set forcing (§3).** The columns of the relation matrix are fixed by quadratic residuosity. They are exactly the primes $r\le B$ for which $N$ is a square modulo $r$.
* **Smooth counts over prime sets (§4).** Exponential upper and lower bounds on $\Psi_S(X)$ in terms of $|S|$, a multiplicative step, and a yield ceiling with exponent $Q(N,B)$.
* **The sign-flip criterion (§5).** One more column costs $+1$ in the relation target and gains multiplicatively in yield. We give a checkable sufficient condition for the cost to fall, and report experiments showing paid work decreasing by $2.4\times$–$13.1\times$ as $Q$ increases.
* **Dickman is blind to $Q$ (§6).** At fixed $u$, Dickman's $\rho(u)$ cannot distinguish moduli. The split ratio $Q/\pi(B)$ can.
* **The direction of the rank bound (§7).** An exact prefix-rank identity and sharpness of $k_{\rm success}\le Q+1$.
* **The $\mathbb{F}_2$-rank trap (§8).** A complete criterion for discriminating test matrices, and one-sidedness of the error.
* **Large primes (§9).** The partial-relation threshold $a+(b-D)>Q$.
* **Methodology (§10).** Instrument faults, mutation testing, and a data-integrity correction.

No new factoring algorithm results. The contribution is a corrected map of which parameters are real levers.

---

## 2. Setting and notation

Throughout, $N$ is a positive integer (in applications an odd composite that is not a perfect square), $B\ge 2$ is the smoothness bound, and $\pi(B)$ is the number of primes $\le B$. The **factor base** is the set $\mathcal{P}_B=\{p\le B: p\text{ prime}\}$.

**Definition 2.1 (sieve value).** For $x\in\mathbb{Z}$, the sieve value is $f(x)=x^2-N$.

**Definition 2.2 (admissible, ramified, split, inert).** A prime $r$ is *admissible for $N$* if $N$ is a square modulo $r$, that is, $N\equiv y^2\pmod r$ for some $y$. An admissible prime with $r\mid N$ is *ramified*. An admissible prime with $r\nmid N$ (equivalently, Legendre symbol $(N/r)=+1$) is *split*. A non-admissible prime is *inert*. We write
$$\mathcal{A}(N,B)=\{r\in\mathcal{P}_B : N \text{ is a square mod } r\},\qquad Q(N,B)=|\mathcal{A}(N,B)|.$$
For $r=2$ every residue is a square, so $2$ is always admissible.

**Definition 2.3 (sieve-reachable primes).** $\mathcal{R}(N,B)=\{r\in\mathcal{P}_B: r\mid f(x)\text{ for some } x\in\mathbb{Z}\}$.

**Definition 2.4 (smooth counts over a prime set).** For a finite set $S$ of primes and $X\ge 0$,
$$\Psi_S(X)=\#\{1\le n\le X:\ \text{every prime factor of } n \text{ lies in } S\}.$$
In particular $\Psi_{\mathcal{P}_B}(X)=\Psi(X,B)$ is the classical count of $B$-smooth integers.

**Definition 2.5 (sieve yield).** For $a\le b$, $\mathrm{yield}(N,B;a,b)=\#\{x\in[a,b]: f(x)\ \text{is } B\text{-smooth}\}$.

**Definition 2.6 (model work).** For a prime set $S$ with $\Psi_S(X)>0$,
$$\mathrm{work}(S;X)=\frac{|S|+1}{\Psi_S(X)}.$$
This is the number of candidates of size $\le X$ examined per guaranteed dependency, under the idealization that the sieve values behave like the integers in $[1,X]$.

**Definition 2.7 (first dependency).** Let $v_0,v_1,v_2,\dots$ be vectors in a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ over a field $K$. For $k\ge 0$ write $\mathrm{pre}_k=(v_0,\dots,v_{k-1})$ and $\operatorname{rk}(k)=\dim\operatorname{span}(\mathrm{pre}_k)$. Define $k_{\rm success}$ as the least $k$ such that $\mathrm{pre}_k$ is linearly dependent. Such a $k$ exists because any $\dim V+1$ vectors are dependent.

---

## 3. Split-set forcing: $Q$ is fixed by the polynomial

**Theorem 3.1 (sieve divisibility forces a split prime).** Let $r$ be prime with $r\nmid N$. If $r\mid x^2-N$ for some integer $x$, then $(N/r)=+1$.

*Proof.* From $r\mid x^2-N$ we get $x^2\equiv N\pmod r$, so $N$ is a square modulo $r$, and it is nonzero modulo $r$ because $r\nmid N$. By definition of the Legendre symbol (Euler's criterion for odd $r$; trivially for $r=2$), $(N/r)=+1$. $\square$

**Theorem 3.2 (the factor base is the split set).** For every $N$ and $B$, $\mathcal{R}(N,B)=\mathcal{A}(N,B)$.

*Proof.* ($\subseteq$) If $r\mid x^2-N$ then $N\equiv x^2\pmod r$. ($\supseteq$) If $N\equiv y^2\pmod r$, take $x=y$: then $r\mid y^2-N$. $\square$

So a prime outside $\mathcal{A}(N,B)$ is never hit by the sieve, and every prime inside is hit, periodically with period $r$.

**Theorem 3.3 (ramified $\cup$ split decomposition).**
$$\mathcal{A}(N,B)=\{r\in\mathcal{P}_B: r\mid N\}\ \cup\ \{r\in\mathcal{P}_B: (N/r)=+1\}.$$

*Proof.* If $r\mid N$ then $N\equiv 0=0^2$. If $r\nmid N$, then $N$ is a square mod $r$ if and only if $(N/r)=+1$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.4 (smoothness is smoothness over the split set).** If $v=x^2-N>0$, then $v$ is $B$-smooth if and only if every prime factor of $v$ lies in $\mathcal{A}(N,B)$.

*Proof.* Every prime factor $r$ of $v$ divides a sieve value, hence lies in $\mathcal{A}(N,\infty)$ by Theorem 3.2. It lies in $\mathcal{P}_B$ exactly when $r\le B$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.5 (exact deficit).** $Q(N,B)+\#\{r\in\mathcal{P}_B:\ r \text{ inert}\}=\pi(B)$. In particular $Q(N,B)\le\pi(B)$.

The columns of the $\mathbb{F}_2$ relation matrix are therefore pinned to $\mathcal{A}(N,B)$. Short of changing $B$ or the polynomial, no design choice can enlarge the column set. The only way to make it smaller is to throw away admissible primes on purpose, and §5 shows that this is counterproductive.

**Example 3.6.** Let $N=103\,764\,863$ and $x=10188$. Then $x^2-N=30\,481=11\cdot17\cdot163$. Theorem 3.1 predicts, and direct computation confirms, $(N/11)=(N/17)=(N/163)=+1$. For this $N$:

| $B$ | $\pi(B)$ | $Q(N,B)$ | inert primes $\le B$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 100 | 25 | 13 | 12 |
| 500 | 95 | 49 | 46 |
| 2000 | 303 | 133 | 170 |

In a real single-polynomial sieve run, all $2\,215$ of $2\,215$ smooth values found had prime support inside the split set, as Theorem 3.2 requires.

**Remark 3.7 (the CRT premise).** A related proposal aimed to control a fraction of the factor base by working modulo a product $R^\#=\prod_{p\le R}p$ via the Chinese Remainder Theorem. For this to be meaningful we need $\theta(R)=\sum_{p\le R}\log p<\ln N$. Since $\theta(R)\sim R$, this forces $R=O(\ln N)$. Hence $\pi(R)/\pi(B)\to0$ for any factor-base bound $B$ growing faster than $\ln N$, which covers every regime of interest. The premise was also excluded by exhaustive enumeration at experimental sizes. We regard it as closed.

---

## 4. Smooth counts over a prime set

**Lemma 4.1 (monotonicity).** If $S\subseteq T$ then $\Psi_S(X)\le\Psi_T(X)$. $\square$

**Proposition 4.2 (multiplicative step).** Let $p$ be a prime with $p\notin S$. Then
$$\Psi_{S\cup\{p\}}(X)\ \ge\ \Psi_S(X)+\Psi_S(\lfloor X/p\rfloor).$$

*Proof.* Let $\mathcal{S}(Y)$ denote the $S$-smooth integers in $[1,Y]$. Map $m\mapsto pm$ from $\mathcal{S}(\lfloor X/p\rfloor)$ into $[1,X]$. The map is injective, and its images are $(S\cup\{p\})$-smooth. They are divisible by $p\notin S$, so they are disjoint from $\mathcal{S}(X)$. Hence $\mathcal{S}(X)$ and $p\cdot\mathcal{S}(\lfloor X/p\rfloor)$ are disjoint subsets of the $(S\cup\{p\})$-smooth integers in $[1,X]$. $\square$

**Proposition 4.3 (exponential floor).** If $S$ consists of primes and $\prod_{p\in S}p\le X$, then $2^{|S|}\le\Psi_S(X)$.

*Proof.* The $2^{|S|}$ square-free products $\prod_{p\in T}p$, for $T\subseteq S$, are distinct by unique factorization. Each is at most $\prod_{p\in S}p\le X$, and each is $S$-smooth. $\square$

**Proposition 4.4 (exponential ceiling).** For every finite prime set $S$ and $X\ge1$,
$$\Psi_S(X)\ \le\ (\lfloor\log_2X\rfloor+1)^{|S|}.$$

*Proof.* An $S$-smooth $n\le X$ is $\prod_{p\in S}p^{e_p}$ with $2^{e_p}\le p^{e_p}\le X$, so $0\le e_p\le\lfloor\log_2X\rfloor$. By unique factorization, $n\mapsto(e_p)_{p\in S}$ is injective into a set of size $(\lfloor\log_2X\rfloor+1)^{|S|}$. $\square$

At a fixed value size $X$ (hence fixed $u$), $\Psi_S(X)$ is therefore squeezed between two functions exponential in $|S|$. The base changes between the two bounds; the exponent is always the size of the prime set.

**Theorem 4.5 (yield ceiling governed by $Q$).** Let $a\le b$ with $a^2>N$. Then
$$\mathrm{yield}(N,B;a,b)\ \le\ \Psi_{\mathcal{A}(N,B)}(b^2-N)\ \le\ \bigl(\lfloor\log_2(b^2-N)\rfloor+1\bigr)^{Q(N,B)}.$$

*Proof.* The map $x\mapsto x^2-N$ is injective on $[a,b]\subset\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, and its values lie in $[1,b^2-N]$ because $a^2>N$. By Corollary 3.4 a $B$-smooth value has all its prime factors in $\mathcal{A}(N,B)$, so it is counted by $\Psi_{\mathcal{A}(N,B)}(b^2-N)$. The second inequality is Proposition 4.4. $\square$

**Remark 4.6.** Take two moduli $N_1,N_2$ of the same size, sieved with the same $B$ over the same window, so that $u$ is the same. Their ceilings differ by the factor $(\lfloor\log_2 X\rfloor+1)^{Q(N_1,B)-Q(N_2,B)}$. Because $Q/\pi(B)$ fluctuates around $1/2$ from one modulus to the next, this factor can be very large. This is the structural shadow of the empirical finding in §6.

---

## 5. The sign-flip criterion: paid work decreases in $Q$

**Theorem 5.1 (criterion).** Let $p\notin S$ with $\Psi_S(X)>0$, and write $S'=S\cup\{p\}$. Then
$$\mathrm{work}(S';X)\le\mathrm{work}(S;X)\iff \Psi_S(X)\ \le\ (|S|+1)\bigl(\Psi_{S'}(X)-\Psi_S(X)\bigr).$$

*Proof.* Since $|S'|=|S|+1$ and both denominators are positive, the inequality $\frac{|S|+2}{\Psi_{S'}}\le\frac{|S|+1}{\Psi_S}$ is equivalent to $(|S|+2)\Psi_S\le(|S|+1)\Psi_{S'}$. Rearranging gives $\Psi_S\le(|S|+1)(\Psi_{S'}-\Psi_S)$. $\square$

**Corollary 5.2 (the sign flip).** If $p$ is a prime not in $S$, $\Psi_S(X)>0$, and
$$(|S|+1)\cdot\Psi_S(\lfloor X/p\rfloor)\ \ge\ \Psi_S(X),$$
then $\mathrm{work}(S\cup\{p\};X)\le\mathrm{work}(S;X)$.

*Proof.* By Proposition 4.2, $\Psi_{S'}(X)-\Psi_S(X)\ge\Psi_S(\lfloor X/p\rfloor)$. Now apply Theorem 5.1. $\square$

Adding a column costs an *additive* $+1$ in the relation target and buys a *multiplicative* gain in the smooth count. The hypothesis of Corollary 5.2 asks only that the $S$-smooth numbers below $X/p$ be at least a $1/(|S|+1)$ fraction of those below $X$. For a small prime $p$ and a moderately large $S$ this is mild.

**Example 5.3.** Take $S=\{2,3\}$, $X=100$, $p=5$. Then $\Psi_{\{2,3\}}(100)=20$ and $\Psi_{\{2,3\}}(20)=10$, and $3\cdot10=30\ge20$. Corollary 5.2 therefore certifies $\mathrm{work}(\{2,3,5\})\le\mathrm{work}(\{2,3\})$ without computing $\Psi_{\{2,3,5\}}$. In fact $\Psi_{\{2,3,5\}}(100)=34$, and $\mathrm{work}(\{2,3,5\})=4/34<3/20=\mathrm{work}(\{2,3\})$ strictly.

**Empirical evidence.** Three independent experimental designs were run, each with cross-validated instruments: a synthetic smoothness model, a CRT-based model, and a real single-polynomial QS. All three reached the same verdict. The number of sieve positions examined, which is the paid cost, decreases monotonically as $Q$ increases, by $2.4\times$ to $13.1\times$ across the range tested depending on the design. The earlier correlation $\operatorname{corr}(Q/\pi(B),k_{\rm success})=+0.77$ is genuine and survives controls, but it describes the number of relations, not the paid work.

A small reproducible instance shows the effect. Take $N=103\,764\,863$ and $B=400$, so $Q(N,B)=41$. Restrict the columns to the $q$ smallest admissible primes and count the positions $x\ge\lceil\sqrt N\rceil$ scanned until $q+1$ relations smooth over those $q$ primes have been found:

| $q$ | 16 | 22 | 28 | 34 | 41 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| positions scanned | 1651 | 784 | 747 | 638 | 599 |

**Design rule 5.4.** *At fixed $B$, the paid sieve length decreases in $Q$. A proposal that shrinks the factor base in order to shrink the linear algebra is moving the wrong term by construction.* The magnitude of the effect depends on $B$, and any quoted ratio should be labelled as a fixed-$B$ number.

---

## 6. The smooth density is governed by $Q$, not by Dickman's $\rho(u)$ alone

Let $\rho$ denote the Dickman function: $\rho(u)=1$ for $0\le u\le1$ and $u\rho'(u)=-\rho(u-1)$ for $u>1$. Classically $\Psi(X,X^{1/u})\sim\rho(u)X$. An earlier round reported that "the Dickman density survives measurement". We refine this claim.

**Empirical finding 6.1.** Across instances compared at matched $u=\log X/\log B$:
$$\operatorname{corr}\bigl(\log\rho(u),\ \text{measured smooth density}\bigr)=+0.029,\qquad \operatorname{corr}\bigl(Q/\pi(B),\ \text{measured smooth density}\bigr)=+0.882.$$

**Interpretation.** $\rho(u)$ correctly predicts how yield depends on $u$, but $u$ alone does not determine the yield across instances. Once $u$ is held fixed, $\rho(u)$ is a constant and carries no information about the variation between moduli. That variation is governed by the split structure of the factor base. Theorem 4.5 and Remark 4.6 give the rigorous counterpart: the yield ceiling has exponent $Q(N,B)$, not $\pi(B)$. The classical heuristic $\Psi(X,B)\approx\rho(u)X$ concerns *all* integers. Sieve values $x^2-N$ are not typical integers, because their prime factors are confined to $\mathcal{A}(N,B)$ (Theorem 3.2), and each admissible odd prime $r\nmid N$ divides a sieve value with frequency $2/r$ rather than $1/r$. The claim that "Dickman survives" is thus true of $u$ but blind to $Q$.

---

## 7. Which way does the rank bound point?

Let $v_0,v_1,\dots$ be the exponent vectors of relations in $V=\mathbb{F}_2^{\mathcal{A}(N,B)}$, so $\dim V=Q$. A disputed chain read "$k_{\rm success}\le\operatorname{rank}+1\le Q+1$". The objection was that the first inequality is backwards. We show that the two readings concern different ranks and that both are correct. Everything in this section holds over an arbitrary field $K$.

**Lemma 7.1.** $\operatorname{rk}(k)\le k$, and $\operatorname{rk}$ is non-decreasing in $k$. Moreover, $\mathrm{pre}_k$ is linearly independent if and only if $\operatorname{rk}(k)=k$. $\square$

**Proposition 7.2 (dependence forces a gap).** If $\mathrm{pre}_k$ is linearly dependent, then $\operatorname{rk}(k)+1\le k$.

*Proof.* Combine $\operatorname{rk}(k)\le k$ with $\operatorname{rk}(k)\ne k$. $\square$

**Theorem 7.3 (prefix-rank identity).**
$$k_{\rm success}=\operatorname{rk}(k_{\rm success})+1.$$

*Proof.* Write $k=k_{\rm success}$. Then $k\ge1$ because the empty family is independent. By Proposition 7.2, $\operatorname{rk}(k)+1\le k$. By minimality, $\mathrm{pre}_{k-1}$ is independent, so $\operatorname{rk}(k-1)=k-1$. By monotonicity, $k-1\le\operatorname{rk}(k)$. $\square$

**Corollary 7.4 (the original chain, for the full collected matrix).** Let $M=\mathrm{pre}_n$ with $n\ge k_{\rm success}$. Then $k_{\rm success}\le\operatorname{rank}(M)+1\le\dim V+1$.

*Proof.* Use Theorem 7.3 together with $\operatorname{rk}(k_{\rm success})\le\operatorname{rk}(n)\le\dim V$. $\square$

**Theorem 7.5 (sharpness).** In $K^Q$, if $v_i=e_i$ is the $i$-th standard basis vector for $0\le i<Q$, then $k_{\rm success}=Q+1$.

*Proof.* $\mathrm{pre}_Q$ is a basis, so every shorter prefix is independent, and $k_{\rm success}\le Q+1$ by Corollary 7.4. $\square$

**Corollary 7.6 (QS form).** For relation vectors in $\mathbb{F}_2^{\mathcal{A}(N,B)}$, the first dependency occurs after at most $Q(N,B)+1$ relations, and exactly one relation after the rank of the prefix it closes.

**Remarks.**

1. The objection is right about the *prefix* rank: dependence at prefix $k$ requires $k>\operatorname{rk}(k)$. The original chain is right about the rank of *all* collected relations. Theorem 7.3 says the two meet at the first dependency.
2. All of these bounds count **relations**. None of them bounds the number of sieve **positions** needed to find $k_{\rm success}$ relations, and that number is the paid work of §5. In particular, $\operatorname{rank}\le Q$ yields a guaranteed nontrivial null vector after $Q+1$ relations, and it gives no upper bound on sieving work.
3. In the corrected experimental run, $k_{\rm success}\le Q+1$ held in $180/180$ instances. An earlier apparent violation was traced to a sieve bug. The measured ratio $k_{\rm success}/Q$ was about $0.78$, $0.71$ and $0.60$ at $B=1024$, $2048$ and $4096$. By Theorem 7.5 these ratios are properties of the instances, not of the algebra. A single "typical" value such as $0.72$ is a mid-range figure, not a constant.

---

## 8. The $\mathbb{F}_2$-rank trap

During the experiments, two rank routines in a widely used computer-algebra library were found to return the rank over $\mathbb{Q}$ when asked for the rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$. One was a general matrix rank; the other explicitly advertises a $\mathrm{GF}(2)$ domain. On a matrix of $\mathbb{F}_2$-rank 2 they returned 3. We explain why such a bug survives ordinary testing, and in which direction it errs.

**Theorem 8.1.** Over any field, a square matrix has full rank if and only if its determinant is nonzero. $\square$

**Corollary 8.2.** Let $A$ be a square integer matrix. Then:
(a) $A$ has full rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$ if and only if $\det A$ is odd;
(b) $A$ has full rank over $\mathbb{Q}$ if and only if $\det A\ne0$.

*Proof.* The determinant commutes with ring homomorphisms. So $\det(A\bmod 2)=\det A\bmod2$, and $\det(A\otimes\mathbb{Q})=\det A$. Now apply Theorem 8.1. $\square$

**Theorem 8.3 (discriminating-test criterion).** For a square integer matrix $A$, the statements "$A$ has full rank over $\mathbb{Q}$" and "$A$ has full rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$" disagree if and only if $\det A$ is a nonzero even integer.

*Proof.* By Corollary 8.2 the two statements are "$\det A\neq0$" and "$\det A$ odd". They agree when $\det A=0$ (both false) and when $\det A$ is odd (both true). They disagree exactly when $\det A$ is nonzero and even. $\square$

So on the full-rank question, a validation suite built from matrices whose determinants are odd or zero cannot detect a routine that computes over $\mathbb{Q}$. Identity matrices, unitriangular matrices and visibly singular matrices all belong to this blind class.

**Example 8.4 (the witness).** Let $T$ be the incidence matrix of a triangle:
$$T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det T=2.$$
Then $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Q}}T=3$ and $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_2}T=2$. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ the three rows sum to zero, and the upper-left $2\times2$ minor equals $1$, which gives the lower bound $2$. (Rank does not increase when passing to an arbitrary submatrix.)

**Lemma 8.5 (2-adic lifting of independence).** Let $v_1,\dots,v_k\in\mathbb{Z}^m$ be vectors whose reductions mod 2 are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Then $v_1,\dots,v_k$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Z}$.

*Proof.* Suppose $\sum g_iv_i=0$ with $g\in\mathbb{Z}^k$. Reducing mod 2 gives a relation over $\mathbb{F}_2$, so every $g_i$ is even. Then $\sum(g_i/2)v_i=0$ is again an integer relation. By induction, $2^j\mid g_i$ for every $j$, which forces $g_i=0$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.6 (one-sided error).** For every integer matrix $A$, $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_2}(A\bmod2)\le\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Q}}(A)$.

*Proof.* Choose columns of $A$ whose reductions form a basis of the $\mathbb{F}_2$-column space. By Lemma 8.5 these columns are $\mathbb{Z}$-independent. Hence they are $\mathbb{Q}$-independent, since clearing denominators turns a rational relation into an integer one. $\square$

**Consequence.** A routine that silently returns the rational rank can only *over*-report the $\mathbb{F}_2$-rank. It therefore under-reports the null space, and its failure mode is a sieve that reports "no dependency yet" while one exists. It never invents a spurious dependency, which is why the bug presents as a puzzling shortage of results rather than as wrong answers.

**Mutation testing.** A validation suite is evidence only if it can fail. Following Theorem 8.3, the experimental pipeline added a mutation test: deliberately broken routines were injected (including a rational-rank routine posing as an $\mathbb{F}_2$-rank routine), and the suite was required to reject them. Both injected mutants were caught. Without this step, "validation passed" is unfalsifiable.

---

## 9. The large-prime channel: more relations, same columns

The open problem left by §§3–5 is the following. *Given a fixed $B$, can the yield collapse be evaded without shrinking the column space?* The first candidate channel is the classical large-prime (partial-relation) variant. We prove its algebraic core.

**Setting 9.1.** Let $A$ be a finite set of primes, the column set, with $|A|=Q$. We are given:

* $a$ **full relations** $F_1,\dots,F_a$: nonzero integers with all prime factors in $A$;
* $b$ **partial relations** $P_i=s_i\ell_i$ ($1\le i\le b$): each $s_i$ is a nonzero integer with prime factors in $A$, and each $\ell_i$ is a prime (the *large prime*, typically in $(B,B^2]$);
* $D=\#\{\ell_1,\dots,\ell_b\}$, the number of **distinct** large primes.

For each $i$, let $\operatorname{rep}(i)$ be the least index $j$ with $\ell_j=\ell_i$. Call $i$ *paired* if $\operatorname{rep}(i)\neq i$.

**Lemma 9.2 (pairing count).** At least $b-D$ indices are paired.

*Proof.* The unpaired indices are the fixed points of $\operatorname{rep}$. The map $i\mapsto\ell_i$ is injective on them, since $\operatorname{rep}$ depends only on $\ell_i$. So there are at most $D$ fixed points. $\square$

**Lemma 9.3 (the large prime cancels).** For each paired $i$,
$$P_i\,P_{\operatorname{rep}(i)}=s_i\,s_{\operatorname{rep}(i)}\,\ell_i^2.$$
$\square$

**Lemma 9.4 (pigeonhole in $\mathbb{F}_2^A$).** Given more than $|A|$ nonzero integers, all with prime factors in $A$, some nonempty subcollection has a product that is a perfect square.

*Proof.* Their exponent vectors mod 2 are more than $\dim\mathbb{F}_2^A$ vectors, so some nonempty subset sums to $0$. The product over that subset has only even exponents. $\square$

**Theorem 9.5 (large-prime congruence of squares).** In Setting 9.1, if
$$Q<a+(b-D),$$
then some nonempty collection of full relations and paired products $P_iP_{\operatorname{rep}(i)}$ multiplies to a perfect square.

*Proof.* Form the combined family: the $a$ full relations, together with the products $P_iP_{\operatorname{rep}(i)}$ for paired $i$. By Lemma 9.2 the family has at least $a+(b-D)>Q$ members. Their *cores*, namely $F_j$ and $s_is_{\operatorname{rep}(i)}$, are nonzero and supported on $A$. By Lemma 9.4 some nonempty subfamily has square core product. By Lemma 9.3, the full product equals that square times $\prod\ell_i^2$, which is again a square. $\square$

**Example 9.6.** Let $A=\{2,3\}$ ($Q=2$), with one full relation $F_1=6$ and partials $2\cdot101$, $3\cdot101$, $6\cdot101$. Then $a=1$, $b=3$, $D=1$, and $a+(b-D)=3>2$. Pairing with the representative gives $P_2P_1=6\cdot101^2$, and
$$6\cdot(3\cdot101)(2\cdot101)=(6\cdot101)^2.$$
Without the partials ($a=1\le Q$) no dependency is guaranteed.

**Interpretation.** The column count stays at $Q$, while the effective relation count grows from $a$ to $a+(b-D)$. This is precisely the sense in which the large-prime channel "evades the yield collapse without shrinking the column space". Whether it is *cheaper* is no longer a linear-algebra question. It reduces to the growth of the collision count $b-D$, which is a weighted birthday problem.

**Conjecture 9.7 (large-prime collision threshold).** Suppose the large primes $\ell_i$ lie in $(B,B^2]$ with probability weight proportional to $1/\ell$. Then the expected collision count $\mathbb{E}[b-D]$ grows quadratically in $b$ until saturation, and the first time $a+(b-D)>Q$ occurs strictly earlier, in sieve positions, than the first time $a>Q$.

A simulation with $B=300$ gives mean collision counts of about $1.2$, $4.3$, $18.7$, $61.9$ and $197.8$ for $b=50$, $100$, $200$, $400$ and $800$, consistent with the predicted early quadratic growth.

---

## 10. Methodology and data integrity

Every instrument fault in this study was caught by cross-checking, never by inspection:

1. **Rank over the wrong field (§8).** Two library routines returned the rational rank.
2. **Modular square roots.** A Tonelli–Shanks implementation passed $4\,692$ random test pairs while carrying two defects.
3. **The gcd step.** A routine halved exponents per relation instead of summing them first. The resulting sieve ran cleanly and reported "no factor" on every instance.
4. **The log-sieve.** A logarithmic sieve without prime-power terms had recall $0.54$, which inflated absolute work by about $2.1\times$. Relative comparisons were unaffected.

A data-integrity issue was also found and corrected. Two experimental reports contained 16-row sample tables that had been transcribed rather than regenerated from the per-instance records. Ten of the sixteen quoted $(p,q)$ rows matched no stored record, one modulus was digit-transposed, and some quoted "ranks" were the ceiling $Q+1$ rather than the measured rank. Every *aggregate* statistic in those reports was exact. The sample tables were withdrawn, and only aggregates are used in this paper. The general rule is that a table that looks primary must be regenerated from primary data.

---

## 11. Algorithms

**Algorithm A (admissible factor base).** *Input:* $N$, $B$. *Output:* $\mathcal{A}(N,B)$.
1. Enumerate the primes $p\le B$ with the sieve of Eratosthenes.
2. For $p=2$, or $p\mid N$, include $p$.
3. Otherwise compute $N^{(p-1)/2}\bmod p$ (Euler's criterion) and include $p$ if the result is $1$.

The cost is $O(\pi(B)\log B)$ modular multiplications. By Theorem 3.2 the output is exactly the set of primes the sieve can hit.

**Algorithm B ($\Psi_S(X)$ by product enumeration).** Recursively enumerate exponent vectors $(e_p)_{p\in S}$ with $\prod p^{e_p}\le X$. The running time is $O(\Psi_S(X))$, which by Proposition 4.4 is at most $(\lfloor\log_2X\rfloor+1)^{|S|}$.

**Algorithm C (first dependency over $\mathbb{F}_2$).** Maintain an XOR basis indexed by pivot bit. For each new exponent vector, reduce it by the basis. If it reduces to $0$, return the current count $k=k_{\rm success}$; otherwise insert it. By Theorem 7.3, the basis size at termination is $k_{\rm success}-1$. The cost is $O(k\,Q^2/w)$ word operations with word size $w$.

**Algorithm D (discriminating test generation).** Draw random small integer square matrices and keep those with $\det$ nonzero and even (Theorem 8.3). Include the triangle witness $T$. Confirm that a rational-rank mutant is rejected before accepting a suite.

**Algorithm E (large-prime pairing).** Hash partials by large prime. Pair each later partial with the first one sharing its large prime. Append each pair's core $s_is_{\operatorname{rep}(i)}$ as a relation. A dependency is guaranteed once $a+(b-D)>Q$ (Theorem 9.5). The running time is linear in $b$.

---

## 12. Discussion and future work

The argument is short to state. Quadratic residuosity fixes the columns (§3). Smooth yield is exponential in the number of columns (§4). Adding a column costs $+1$ but gains a multiplicative factor (§5). Hence, at fixed $B$, the optimal factor base is as large as the method allows. Classical Dickman heuristics describe dependence on $u$ but say nothing about the variation in $Q$ between moduli (§6). The linear-algebra bound $k_{\rm success}\le Q+1$ is correct, sharp and exactly characterized (§7), but it bounds relations, not work.

**Open problem.** At fixed $B$, evade the yield collapse without shrinking the column space. The candidate channels are:
1. **Large primes and partial relations** (§9). The algebra is settled; the remaining task is to price the collision statistics (Conjecture 9.7). Double-large-prime variants lead to cycle counting in a graph on large primes.
2. **Multi-polynomial sieving.** Many polynomials $(\alpha x+\beta)^2-N$ keep the value size small. It remains to determine whether the split-set forcing of §3 transfers polynomial by polynomial. It should, since every such value is $\equiv$ a square minus $N$ modulo each prime, and therefore $Q$ remains the column count.
3. **Per-instance adaptive $B$.** Raising $B$ raises $Q$. Whether the penalty is escapable depends on the joint growth of $\Psi$ and $Q$ in $B$, which could be modelled with Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 5.2.

All three lie outside the single-polynomial regime analysed here. Consistent with every earlier round of this investigation, no new factoring method results. What does result is that one popular lever (shrinking $Q$) is disproved, one heuristic (Dickman alone) is sharpened, one inequality is oriented correctly, and one class of silent software faults is characterized completely.

---

def primes_upto(n: int) -> list[int]:
    """Sieve of Eratosthenes."""

def factorize(n: int) -> dict[int, int]:
    """Trial-division factorisation of a positive integer."""
    out: dict[int, int] = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            out[d] = out.get(d, 0) + 1
            n //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2
    if n > 1:
        out[n] = out.get(n, 0) + 1
    return out


def legendre(a: int, p: int) -> int:
    """Legendre symbol (a/p) for an odd prime p; for p = 2 returns 1 if a odd, 0 if even."""
    a %= p
    if a == 0:
        return 0
    if p == 2:
        return 1
    return 1 if pow(a, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1 else -1


def is_square_mod(a: int, p: int) -> bool:
    """Is a a square modulo the prime p (zero counts as a square)?"""
    return a % p == 0 or legendre(a, p) == 1


def admissible_primes(N: int, B: int) -> list[int]:
    """Primes p <= B with N a square mod p: the ramified and split primes."""
    return [p for p in primes_upto(B) if is_square_mod(N, p)]


def sieve_reachable(N: int, B: int) -> list[int]:
    """Primes p <= B dividing x^2 - N for SOME x (checked over one full period)."""
    return [p for p in primes_upto(B) if any((x * x - N) % p == 0 for x in range(p))]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Smooth counting over a prime set
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def psi_S(S: Iterable[int], X: int) -> int:
    """Number of n in [1, X] all of whose prime factors lie in S (by enumeration of products)."""
    primes = sorted(set(S))
    count = 0

    def rec(i: int, cur: int) -> None:
        nonlocal count
        if i == len(primes):
            count += 1
            return
        p = primes[i]
        v = cur
        while v <= X:
            rec(i + 1, v)
            v *= p

    rec(0, 1)
    return count


def model_work(S: Sequence[int], X: int) -> Fraction:
    """Model cost (|S| + 1) / Psi_S(X): positions per guaranteed dependence."""
    return Fraction(len(S) + 1, psi_S(S, X))


def is_smooth_over(v: int, S: set[int]) -> bool:
    """Is v > 0 composed only of primes in S?"""
    if v <= 0:
        return False
    for p in S:
        while v % p == 0:
            v //= p
    return v == 1


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Linear algebra over GF(2) and over Q
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def rank_gf2(rows: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> int:
    """Rank over GF(2) via XOR elimination on bit-packed rows."""
    basis: dict[int, int] = {}  # pivot bit -> row
    for row in rows:
        v = 0
        for j, a in enumerate(row):
            if a % 2:
                v |= 1 << j
        while v:
            h = v.bit_length() - 1
            if h in basis:
                v ^= basis[h]
            else:
                basis[h] = v
                break
    return len(basis)


def rank_rational(rows: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> int:
    """Exact rank over Q via fraction-based Gaussian elimination."""
    M = [[Fraction(a) for a in r] for r in rows]
    if not M:
        return 0
    rank, ncols = 0, len(M[0])
    for c in range(ncols):
        piv = next((i for i in range(rank, len(M)) if M[i][c] != 0), None)
        if piv is None:
            continue
        M[rank], M[piv] = M[piv], M[rank]
        for i in range(len(M)):
            if i != rank and M[i][c] != 0:
                f = M[i][c] / M[rank][c]
                M[i] = [a - f * b for a, b in zip(M[i], M[rank])]
        rank += 1
    return rank


def det_int(rows: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> int:
    """Exact integer determinant (Bareiss fraction-free elimination)."""
    M = [list(r) for r in rows]
    n = len(M)
    sign, prev = 1, 1
    for k in range(n - 1):
        if M[k][k] == 0:
            sw = next((i for i in range(k + 1, n) if M[i][k] != 0), None)
            if sw is None:
                return 0
            M[k], M[sw] = M[sw], M[k]
            sign = -sign
        for i in range(k + 1, n):
            for j in range(k + 1, n):
                M[i][j] = (M[i][j] * M[k][k] - M[i][k] * M[k][j]) // prev
        prev = M[k][k]
    return sign * M[n - 1][n - 1]


def k_success(vectors: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> int:
    """Length of the shortest linearly dependent prefix over GF(2)."""
    for k in range(1, len(vectors) + 1):
        if rank_gf2(vectors[:k]) < k:
            return k
    raise ValueError("no dependent prefix among the supplied vectors")

    results: list[tuple[int, int]] = []
    for frac in (0.4, 0.55, 0.7, 0.85, 1.0):

        for (y, w) in smooth_full:
            if is_smooth_over(w, S):

    demo_paid_work_decreases()
    demo_prefix_rank()
    demo_gf2_trap()
    demo_large_primes()

    main()

    for k in range(1, 8):
        S = ps[:k]
        if math.prod(S) > X:
            break

        print(f"  |S|={k}: {lo:6d} <= {val:7d} <= {hi:12d}")


def demo_paid_work_decreases() -> None:
    banner("3. Paid sieve work at fixed B DECREASES as the column set grows")
    N = 103764863
    B = 400
    A = admissible_primes(N, B)
    a = math.isqrt(N) + 1
    # Precompute factorisations along a long window once.
    window = 400000
    vals = [(y, y * y - N) for y in range(a, a + window)]
    Aset = set(A)

    print(f"N = {N}, B = {B}, Q(N,B) = {len(A)}; smooth values in window: {len(smooth_full)}")
    print("Using only the q smallest admissible primes as columns:")
    print("   q   positions examined to collect q+1 relations")
    results: list[tuple[int, int]] = []
    for frac in (0.4, 0.55, 0.7, 0.85, 1.0):
        q = max(3, int(frac * len(A)))

        needed, seen = q + 1, 0
        pos = None
        for (y, w) in smooth_full:
            if is_smooth_over(w, S):
                seen += 1
                if seen == needed:
                    pos = y - a + 1
                    break
        results.append((q, pos if pos is not None else -1))

def demo_prefix_rank() -> None:
    banner("4. Prefix-rank identity:  k_success = rank(prefix k_success) + 1 <= Q + 1")
    rng = random.Random(42)
    for Q in (8, 16, 32):
        ks = []
        for _ in range(200):
            vecs = [[1 if rng.random() < 0.15 else 0 for _ in range(Q)] for _ in range(3 * Q)]

            assert k == rank_gf2(vecs[:k]) + 1 and k <= Q + 1
            assert k <= rank_gf2(vecs) + 1  # original chain with the FULL collected rank
            ks.append(k)
        print(f"Q = {Q:2d}: identity held 200/200; mean k_success/Q = {sum(ks) / len(ks) / Q:.2f}, "
              f"max = {max(ks)}")
    Q = 10
    basis = [[1 if j == i else 0 for j in range(Q)] for i in range(Q)] + [[1] * Q]
    print(f"Sharpness: standard basis first in GF(2)^{Q} gives k_success = {k_success(basis)} = Q + 1")


def demo_gf2_trap() -> None:
    banner("5. The GF(2)-rank trap")
    trap = [[1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1]]
    print(f"Triangle incidence matrix {trap}: det = {det_int(trap)}, "
          f"rank_Q = {rank_rational(trap)}, rank_GF2 = {rank_gf2(trap)}")
    rng = random.Random(7)
    disc = blind = 0
    for _ in range(2000):
        M = [[rng.randint(0, 1) for _ in range(4)] for _ in range(4)]
        d = det_int(M)
        full_q, full_2 = rank_rational(M) == 4, rank_gf2(M) == 4
        assert (full_q != full_2) == (d != 0 and d % 2 == 0)
        assert rank_gf2(M) <= rank_rational(M)
        disc += (d != 0 and d % 2 == 0)
        blind += not (d != 0 and d % 2 == 0)
    print(f"2000 random 0/1 4x4 matrices: criterion 'disagree <=> det nonzero even' held 2000/2000;")
    print(f"   discriminating test matrices: {disc}, blind ones: {blind}; rank_GF2 <= rank_Q always")
    # Mutation test: a deliberately wrong 'GF(2) rank' (actually rank over Q).
    suite_blind = [[[1, 0], [0, 1]], [[1, 1], [0, 1]], [[1, 1], [1, 1]]]
    suite_good = suite_blind + [trap]
    wrong = rank_rational
    for name, suite in (("odd/zero-det suite", suite_blind), ("suite with det=2 witness", suite_good)):
        caught = any(wrong(M) != rank_gf2(M) for M in suite)
        print(f"   mutation (Q-rank posing as GF(2)-rank) caught by {name}: {caught}")


def demo_large_primes() -> None:
    banner("6. Large-prime pairing: a + (b - D) > Q forces a square, same column space")
    A = [2, 3]
    full = [6]
    partials = [(2, 101), (3, 101), (6, 101)]  # (A-part s, large prime l)
    D = len({l for _, l in partials})
    a, b, Q = len(full), len(partials), len(A)
    print(f"Q = {Q}, a = {a}, b = {b}, D = {D}: a + (b - D) = {a + b - D} > Q ? {a + b - D > Q}")
    rep: dict[int, int] = {}
    combined: list[tuple[str, int]] = [(f"F{j}", f) for j, f in enumerate(full)]
    for i, (s, l) in enumerate(partials):
        if l in rep:
            j = rep[l]
            combined.append((f"P{i}*P{j}", s * l * partials[j][0] * l))
        else:
            rep[l] = i
    for T in range(1, len(combined) + 1):
        for sub in combinations(combined, T):
            prod = math.prod(v for _, v in sub)
            if math.isqrt(prod) ** 2 == prod:
                print(f"Square found: {' * '.join(n for n, _ in sub)} = {prod} = {math.isqrt(prod)}^2")
                break
        else:
            continue
        break
    # Birthday-type growth of b - D for large primes in (B, B^2] with weight ~ 1/l.
    rng = random.Random(1)
    B = 300
    big = [p for p in primes_upto(B * B) if p > B]
    weights = [1 / p for p in big]
    print("\nCollisions b - D among b partials (large primes in (B, B^2], weight ~ 1/l), B = 300:")
    for b2 in (50, 100, 200, 400, 800):
        trials = []
        for _ in range(40):
            ls = rng.choices(big, weights=weights, k=b2)
            trials.append(b2 - len(set(ls)))
        print(f"  b = {b2:4d}: mean (b - D) = {sum(trials) / len(trials):7.2f}")


def main() -> None:
    demo_split_set_forcing()
    demo_smooth_counts()
    demo_paid_work_decreases()
    demo_prefix_rank()
    demo_gf2_trap()
    demo_large_primes()

    main()

algorithms.name: Admissible Factor Base via Euler's Criterion (Split-Set Construction)
algorithms.description: Builds the exact set of primes p <= B that can ever divide a sieve value x^2 - N. By split-set forcing, a prime p not dividing N divides some x^2 - N if and only if the Legendre symbol (N/p) = +1; primes dividing N (ramified) and p = 2 are always included. Inert primes are provably never hit, so they are never columns. Complexity: O(B log log B) for the prime sieve plus O(pi(B) log B) modular multiplications for Euler's criterion. The output size Q(N,B) is the column dimension of the GF(2) relation matrix, and it fixes the exponent in the yield ceiling.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: integer N, bound B
OUTPUT: admissible set A(N,B) and Q = |A|
1. P <- primes up to B (sieve of Eratosthenes)
2. A <- empty list
3. FOR each p in P:
4.     r <- N mod p
5.     IF p = 2 OR r = 0 THEN append p to A            // always / ramified
6.     ELSE IF r^((p-1)/2) mod p = 1 THEN append p to A  // split
7.     // otherwise p is inert: it divides no x^2 - N
8. RETURN A, |A|

algorithms.name: Sign-Flip Certificate for Enlarging the Factor Base
algorithms.description: Decides, in the cost model work(S) = (|S|+1)/Psi_S(X), whether adjoining a prime p to the column set S can be certified not to increase the work, using only counts over S. The certificate (|S|+1) * Psi_S(floor(X/p)) >= Psi_S(X) suffices because of the multiplicative step Psi_{S+p}(X) >= Psi_S(X) + Psi_S(X/p). The exact criterion Psi_S(X) <= (|S|+1)(Psi_{S+p}(X) - Psi_S(X)) is also evaluated. Psi_S is computed by recursive enumeration of exponent vectors in time O(Psi_S(X)), bounded by (log2 X + 1)^|S|.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: prime set S, prime p not in S, size X
OUTPUT: certified (bool), exact (bool), work before/after
1. psi  <- PSI(S, X); psiQ <- PSI(S, floor(X/p))
2. certified <- (|S|+1) * psiQ >= psi
3. psi' <- PSI(S + {p}, X)
4. exact <- psi <= (|S|+1) * (psi' - psi)
5. RETURN certified, exact, (|S|+1)/psi, (|S|+2)/psi'

PSI(S, X): count products prod p_i^{e_i} <= X by depth-first enumeration

algorithms.name: Incremental GF(2) Basis and First-Dependency Detection
algorithms.description: Processes exponent-parity vectors one at a time, maintaining an XOR basis keyed by pivot bit. The first vector that reduces to zero marks k_success, the length of the shortest dependent prefix. By the prefix-rank identity, the basis size at that moment is exactly k_success - 1, and k_success <= Q + 1 with equality attainable. Tracking the combination of original rows that produced the zero vector yields the actual subset whose product is a square. Complexity: O(k Q^2 / w) word operations for k vectors of length Q on a w-bit machine. Unlike generic rank routines, this works natively over GF(2) and cannot silently compute a rational rank.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: stream of parity vectors v_0, v_1, ... in GF(2)^Q (bit-packed)
OUTPUT: k_success and a dependent subset T
1. basis <- empty map pivot -> (vector, combination)
2. FOR k = 1, 2, ...:
3.     (v, c) <- (v_{k-1}, {k-1})
4.     WHILE v != 0 AND top(v) in basis: (v, c) <- (v XOR basis[top].vec, c XOR basis[top].comb)
5.     IF v = 0 THEN RETURN k, c        // assert |basis| = k - 1
6.     basis[top(v)] <- (v, c)

algorithms.name: Discriminating Test-Suite Generation and Mutation Check for GF(2) Rank
algorithms.description: Generates validation matrices that provably detect a rank routine silently computing over the rationals. For a square integer matrix, full GF(2)-rank holds iff det is odd and full Q-rank iff det != 0, so the two verdicts differ iff det is a nonzero even integer. The generator keeps only such matrices (plus the triangle witness with det = 2), and then runs a mutation test: a deliberately wrong routine must be rejected, otherwise the suite is declared unfalsifiable. Determinants use fraction-free Bareiss elimination, O(n^3) exact integer operations.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: size n, count m, candidate routine R
OUTPUT: suite, verdict on R, mutation-test status
1. suite <- [T_triangle]
2. WHILE |suite| < m: draw random small integer n x n matrix M; IF det M != 0 AND det M even: append M
3. mutant <- rank over Q
4. ASSERT exists M in suite with mutant(M) != rank_GF2(M)   // suite can fail
5. RETURN suite, all(R(M) = rank_GF2(M) for M in suite)

algorithms.name: Large-Prime Pairing into the Same Column Space
algorithms.description: Turns partial relations s_i * l_i (s_i smooth over the column set A, l_i a single large prime) into full relations without adding columns. Partials are bucketed by large prime; each later partial is paired with the first (representative) partial sharing its large prime, giving s_i s_rep(i) l_i^2, whose large prime appears squared. At least b - D pairs arise (D = number of distinct large primes), so a congruence of squares is guaranteed as soon as a + (b - D) > Q. Runs in O(b) expected time with hashing; the cost question reduces to the growth of the collision count b - D, a weighted birthday problem.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: full relations F_1..F_a, partials (s_i, l_i) for i=1..b, column count Q
OUTPUT: combined relation list, guarantee flag
1. rep <- empty hash map; combined <- [F_1..F_a]
2. FOR i = 1..b:
3.     IF l_i in rep: j <- rep[l_i]; append core s_i * s_j (value s_i s_j l_i^2) to combined
4.     ELSE rep[l_i] <- i
5. D <- |rep|
6. RETURN combined, (a + (b - D) > Q)

The exponent is the size of the prime set, which is why the sieve yield is governed by Q(N,B) rather than pi(B).

import math
from typing import Iterable
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def primes_upto(n: int) -> list[int]:
    is_p = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    is_p[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if is_p[i]:
            is_p[i * i:: i] = bytearray(len(is_p[i * i:: i]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if is_p[i]]


def is_square_mod(a: int, p: int) -> bool:
    a %= p
    return a == 0 or p == 2 or pow(a, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1


def psi_S(S: list[int], X: int) -> int:
    count = 0

    def rec(i: int, cur: int) -> None:
        nonlocal count
        if i == len(S):
            count += 1
            return
        v = cur
        while v <= X:
            rec(i + 1, v)
            v *= S[i]

    rec(0, 1)
    return count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    X = 10 ** 6
    ps = primes_upto(60)
    ks, lo, mid, hi = [], [], [], []
    for k in range(1, 12):
        S = ps[:k]
        ks.append(k)
        mid.append(psi_S(S, X))
        hi.append((int(math.log2(X)) + 1) ** k)
        lo.append(2 ** k if math.prod(S) <= X else float("nan"))
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
    ax.semilogy(ks, hi, "r--", label=r"ceiling $(\lfloor\log_2 X\rfloor+1)^{|S|}$")
    ax.semilogy(ks, mid, "ko-", label=r"$\Psi_S(X)$, $S$ = first $|S|$ primes")
    ax.semilogy(ks, lo, "g--", label=r"floor $2^{|S|}$ (valid while $\prod S\le X$)")
    ax.set_xlabel("|S|  (size of the prime set)")
    ax.set_ylabel("count")
    ax.set_title(r"Smooth counts are squeezed between exponentials in $|S|$  ($X=10^6$)")
    ax.legend()
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("psi_sandwich.png", dpi=150)
    plt.show()

interactive_layout:
# The Split Set Decides

*An interactive tour of why shrinking the quadratic sieve makes it slower.*

The [quadratic sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_sieve) factors a number $N$ by collecting many values of $x^2 - N$ that factor completely over small primes, then combining them with linear algebra over the two-element field $\mathbb{F}_2$ into a congruence of squares $X^2 \equiv Y^2 \pmod N$.

One idea looks like it should save effort: use fewer primes (fewer **columns**, $Q$), so that fewer relations are needed. This page shows, step by step and with experiments you can run yourself, that the idea points the wrong way.

<details><summary>Background: why a congruence of squares factors N</summary>

If $X^2 \equiv Y^2 \pmod N$ but $X \not\equiv \pm Y$, then $N \mid (X-Y)(X+Y)$ while dividing neither factor. Hence $\gcd(X-Y, N)$ is a proper divisor of $N$. The sieve manufactures such pairs. Each relation $x_i^2 - N = \prod p^{e_{i,p}}$ gives a parity vector $(e_{i,p} \bmod 2)_p$. A set of relations whose parity vectors sum to zero has a perfect-square product, and it supplies $Y$. See also [Dixon's factorization method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixon%27s_factorization_method).
</details>

---

## 1. The sieve chooses its own columns

Start with a simple question: which primes can divide $x^2 - N$ at all? If $r \mid x^2 - N$, then $x^2 \equiv N \pmod r$, so $N$ is a square mod $r$. In terms of the [Legendre symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_symbol), $(N/r) = +1$ whenever $r \nmid N$.

> **Theorem (split-set forcing).** The primes $\le B$ that divide some $x^2-N$ are *exactly* the admissible primes: the ramified ones ($r \mid N$) and the split ones ($(N/r)=+1$). Inert primes, those with $(N/r)=-1$, never appear. Hence $Q(N,B) = \pi(B) - \#\{\text{inert } r \le B\}$.

Open the first tab of the laboratory below. Type in your own $N$, and check that no red (inert) prime ever shows up in a smooth sieve value.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details><summary>Proof of split-set forcing</summary>

($\Rightarrow$) If $r \mid x^2 - N$ then $N \equiv x^2 \pmod r$. ($\Leftarrow$) If $N \equiv y^2 \pmod r$, put $x = y$. For $r \nmid N$, "$N$ is a nonzero square mod $r$" is the definition of $(N/r)=+1$ (by Euler's criterion for odd $r$). Corollary: a positive sieve value is $B$-smooth if and only if all its prime factors are admissible primes $\le B$.
</details>

The algorithm that builds this factor base takes only a few lines, and by the theorem its output is exactly the set of primes the sieve can hit:

{{algorithm:0}}

**Takeaway.** $Q$ is not a free design parameter. Once you fix the polynomial and $B$, the columns are fixed too. The only way to make $Q$ smaller is to throw away good primes on purpose.

---

## 2. Smooth numbers grow exponentially in the number of primes

Let $\Psi_S(X)$ count the integers in $[1, X]$ whose prime factors all lie in a set $S$ (see [smooth numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_number)). Three elementary facts drive everything that follows:

$$2^{|S|} \le \Psi_S(X) \le (\lfloor \log_2 X\rfloor + 1)^{|S|}, \qquad \Psi_{S\cup\{p\}}(X) \ge \Psi_S(X) + \Psi_S(\lfloor X/p \rfloor).$$

The lower bound needs $\prod S \le X$.

{{visualization:1}}

<details><summary>Proofs of the floor, the ceiling and the multiplicative step</summary>

*Floor:* the $2^{|S|}$ square-free products of subsets of $S$ are distinct and at most $\prod S \le X$.
*Ceiling:* an $S$-smooth $n \le X$ is $\prod p^{e_p}$ with $2^{e_p} \le X$, so each exponent takes at most $\lfloor\log_2 X\rfloor+1$ values, and unique factorization makes $n \mapsto (e_p)$ injective.
*Multiplicative step:* $m \mapsto pm$ sends the $S$-smooth numbers $\le X/p$ to new $(S\cup\{p\})$-smooth numbers $\le X$. These are divisible by $p \notin S$, so none of them was counted already.
</details>

Applied to the sieve, this gives the **yield ceiling**: on a window $[a,b]$ with $a^2 > N$,

$$\#\{x\in[a,b] : x^2-N \text{ is } B\text{-smooth}\} \le (\lfloor\log_2(b^2-N)\rfloor+1)^{Q(N,B)}.$$

The exponent is $Q(N,B)$, not $\pi(B)$.

---

## 3. The sign flip: one more column is cheap

Model the cost as "candidates per guaranteed dependency":

$$\mathrm{work}(S) = \frac{|S|+1}{\Psi_S(X)}.$$

Adding a prime raises the numerator by **one** and multiplies the denominator. Combined with the multiplicative step, a little algebra gives:

> **Sign-flip criterion.** If $p \notin S$ and $(|S|+1)\,\Psi_S(\lfloor X/p\rfloor) \ge \Psi_S(X)$, then $\mathrm{work}(S\cup\{p\}) \le \mathrm{work}(S)$.

Example: $S=\{2,3\}$, $X=100$. Here $\Psi_S(100)=20$ and $\Psi_S(20)=10$, and $3\cdot 10 \ge 20$, so adding $5$ is certified to help. Indeed the work drops from $3/20$ to $4/34$. Use **tab ③** of the laboratory to try other sets and sizes.

<details><summary>Proof of the exact criterion</summary>

With $S' = S \cup \{p\}$, the inequality $\frac{|S|+2}{\Psi_{S'}} \le \frac{|S|+1}{\Psi_S}$ is equivalent to $(|S|+2)\Psi_S \le (|S|+1)\Psi_{S'}$, which rearranges to $\Psi_S \le (|S|+1)(\Psi_{S'} - \Psi_S)$. The multiplicative step gives $\Psi_{S'}-\Psi_S \ge \Psi_S(\lfloor X/p\rfloor)$.
</details>

{{algorithm:1}}

Now check it on a real sieve. **Tab ②** of the laboratory and the plot below keep only the $q$ smallest admissible primes and count the positions scanned until $q+1$ relations appear. Every curve goes *down* as $q$ grows. In the full experiments with three independent designs, the paid work fell by $2.4\times$ to $13.1\times$ as $Q$ increased.

{{visualization:0}}

> **Design rule.** At fixed $B$, paid sieve length decreases in $Q$. Shrinking the factor base to shrink the linear algebra moves the wrong term.

---

## 4. Dickman cannot see $Q$

The classical heuristic says a random number near $X$ is $X^{1/u}$-smooth with probability about $\rho(u)$, where $\rho$ is the [Dickman function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function). Across instances compared at *matched* $u$, the measured smooth density correlated with $\log\rho(u)$ at only $+0.029$, but with the split ratio $Q/\pi(B)$ at $+0.882$.

The reason is that at fixed $u$, $\rho(u)$ is a single number, so it cannot explain why two moduli of the same size behave differently. The yield ceiling above can: its exponent is $Q(N,B)$. Sieve values are not typical integers, because their prime factors are confined to the split set, and each odd split prime divides them twice as often as it divides a random integer.

---

## 5. Which way does the rank bound point?

Let $k_{\text{success}}$ be the length of the shortest run of relations that contains a dependency. A disputed chain read $k_{\text{success}} \le \mathrm{rank}+1 \le Q+1$, and the objection was that the first step is backwards. Both sides turn out to be right, about different ranks:

> **Prefix-rank identity.** $k_{\text{success}} = \mathrm{rank}(\text{first } k_{\text{success}} \text{ relations}) + 1.$ Consequently $k_{\text{success}} \le \mathrm{rank}(M)+1 \le Q+1$ for the matrix $M$ of *all* collected relations, and $Q+1$ is attained when the first $Q$ relations are the standard basis.

<details><summary>Proof</summary>

Write $k = k_{\text{success}}$. Since $\text{pre}_k$ is dependent, its rank is at most $k-1$. By minimality $\text{pre}_{k-1}$ is independent, so it has rank $k-1$, and rank only grows when vectors are added. Together these give $\mathrm{rank}(\text{pre}_k) = k-1$. For $M \supseteq \text{pre}_k$, monotonicity gives the original chain.
</details>

{{visualization:2}}

{{algorithm:2}}

These bounds count **relations**, not sieve **positions**. They give a guaranteed square after $Q+1$ relations, but no upper bound on how long it takes to find them.

---

## 6. The bug that honest tests cannot see

Two widely used rank routines returned the rank over $\mathbb{Q}$ when asked for the rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$. On the triangle matrix they report $3$, although over $\mathbb{F}_2$ the rows sum to zero and the rank is $2$.

> **Discriminating-test criterion.** For a square integer matrix, full rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$ means $\det$ is odd, and full rank over $\mathbb{Q}$ means $\det \neq 0$. The two verdicts disagree **iff $\det$ is a nonzero even integer**. Moreover $\mathrm{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_2} \le \mathrm{rank}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ always, so a rational-rank bug can only *hide* dependencies, never invent them.

Try **tab ④** of the laboratory. The identity matrix is "blind" (odd determinant), and the triangle catches the bug ($\det = 2$).

<details><summary>Why the error is one-sided (2-adic descent)</summary>

Suppose integer vectors are independent mod 2 but satisfy $\sum g_i v_i = 0$ over $\mathbb{Z}$. Reducing mod 2 shows that every $g_i$ is even. Divide by 2 and repeat. Each $g_i$ is then divisible by every power of 2, so $g_i = 0$. Independent columns mod 2 therefore stay independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.
</details>

{{algorithm:3}}

A test suite counts as evidence only if it can fail. Injecting a deliberately broken routine (a **mutation test**) and requiring the suite to reject it is what turned "validation passed" into a falsifiable claim.

---

## 7. Where to go next: large primes

At a fixed $B$, can one avoid the yield collapse without shrinking the column space? Partial relations $s\cdot\ell$, with one large prime $\ell > B$, are useless alone. But two partials sharing $\ell$ multiply to $s_1 s_2 \ell^2$, and $\ell^2$ is already a square.

> **Large-prime congruence.** With $a$ full relations, $b$ partials and $D$ distinct large primes, $Q < a + (b-D)$ already forces a perfect-square product in the **same** $\mathbb{F}_2^Q$ column space.

Example: $6\cdot(3\cdot 101)(2\cdot 101) = (6\cdot 101)^2$.

{{algorithm:4}}

The cost question is now a [birthday problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthday_problem): how fast do collisions $b-D$ accumulate? Run **tab ⑤** of the laboratory, or look at the curves below.

{{visualization:3}}

<details><summary>Open conjecture</summary>

If large primes lie in $(B, B^2]$ with weight $\propto 1/\ell$, then $\mathbb{E}[b-D]$ grows quadratically in $b$ until saturation, and the first time $a+(b-D) > Q$ comes strictly earlier, in sieve positions, than the first time $a > Q$.
</details>

---
